newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia Kirishi oil refinery sees higher '97 output.
newsitem.headline: Russia Kirishi oil refinery sees higher '97 output.

text.p: OOO Kirishinefteorgsintez (KINEF), one of Russia's biggest oil refineries, plans to process 16.2 million tonnes of crude oil in 1997, up six percent from the 15.3 million it processed in 1996, a senior company official said.

Nikolai Laptev, KINEF's financial director, told Reuters in an interview at the plant late on Tuesday that this year's planned throughput was close to the plant's nameplate capacity of 16.5-17.0 million tonnes.
"We plan to process 16.2 million tonnes of oil this year, close to the plant's capacity of 16.5 million tonnes," he said.
Other plant officials said KINEF's nameplate capacity was closer to 17.0 million tonnes, but that during the Soviet era it had been known to process as much as 23 million tonnes a year.

Laptev added that the final amount the plant processed would depend on how much crude oil the refinery is fed by OAO Surgutneftegaz, the production arm of KINEF's owner Surgut Holding (NK Surgutneftegaz).
Surgutneftegaz ensures around 80 percent of the refinery's crude oil, and the rest is supplied by trading companies.
The final figure would also depend on how much oil the plant can buy from trading firms, and on domestic and international oil product prices during the course of 1997, he said.
"Of course a lot depends on the quantities of crude oil coming directly from Surgutneftegaz and from others," he said.

The refinery, strategically placed in the northwest of Russia and close to Western markets, produced 4.95 million tonnes of heavy fuel oil last year and 0.83 million of bunker fuel, making fuel oil by far its most important product.
Laptev did not give forecasts for different products in 1997.

Officials said between 65 and 72 percent of the plant's products go abroad, and that the bulk of exports move through the Baltic ports of Ventspils, Riga and Klaipeda, with smaller amounts moving through St Petersburg in Russia.
Laptev said that low fuel oil prices on Western product markets were not too worrying for the plant at this stage.
"For us, prices in the west are not unexpected for this time of year," he said.
But Laptev added that the refinery wanted to boost volumes of light, value-added products, in order to reduce its dependence on cheaper fuel oil over the long term.
The refinery plans to build a hydro-cracking unit to process more fuel oil into light products, but must first raise around $750 million in foreign investment to do so.
"We need to hurry along with the hydrocracker unit," he said.
